paragraphs: In the present state of society it seems necessary to go back to first principles in search of the simplest truths, and to contest every inch of ground with some prevailing prejudice. To clear my way, I must be allowed to ask a few plain questions; and the answers will probably seem as unambiguous as the axioms on which reasoning is built — though, when they become entangled with various motives for action, they are expressly contradicted by men’s words or conduct.
In what does man’s superiority over the animal creation consist? The answer is as clear as the fact that a half is less than the whole: in Reason.
What attainment raises one being above another? Virtue, we reply without a moment’s thought.
For what purpose were the passions implanted in us? So that man, by struggling with them, might attain a degree of knowledge denied to the animals: so whispers Experience.

Consequently, the perfection of our nature and our capacity for happiness must be measured by the degree of reason, virtue and knowledge that distinguishes the individual and directs the laws that bind society together. And it is equally undeniable, if mankind is viewed as a whole, that knowledge and virtue flow naturally from the exercise of reason.

With the rights and duties of man thus reduced to their simplest form, it seems almost impertinent to try to illustrate truths that appear so indisputable. Yet such deep-rooted prejudices have clouded reason, and such counterfeit qualities have taken the name of virtues, that it is necessary to follow the course of reason as it has been confused and entangled in error by various chance circumstances, comparing the simple axiom with the accidental departures from it.

Men in general seem to use their reason to justify prejudices they have absorbed without knowing how, rather than to root them out. It takes a strong mind to form its own principles resolutely, for a kind of intellectual cowardice prevails that makes many men shrink from the task, or do it only halfway. Yet the imperfect conclusions reached in this way are often very plausible, because they rest on partial experience — on views that are accurate, though narrow.

When we go back to first principles, vice, in all its native ugliness, slinks away from close examination; but a set of shallow reasoners are forever exclaiming that such arguments prove too much, and that a measure rotten at the core may still be expedient. So expediency is constantly set against simple principles, until truth is lost in a fog of words, virtue in outward forms, and knowledge is turned into an empty noise by the plausible prejudices that take its name.

That the wisest form of society is the one whose constitution is founded on the nature of man strikes every thinking being so forcibly, in the abstract, that it seems presumptuous to try to offer proofs. Yet proof must be offered, or reason will never storm the stronghold of prescription; and to cite prescription as an argument for depriving men (or women) of their natural rights is one of the absurd sophistries that insult common sense every day.

The civilization of most of the people of Europe is very partial; indeed, it may be questioned whether, in exchange for their innocence, they have gained any virtues that make up for the misery produced by the vices plastered over their unsightly ignorance, and for the freedom they have traded for splendid slavery. The desire to dazzle by wealth, the surest pre-eminence a man can obtain, the pleasure of commanding flattering sycophants, and many other intricate, base calculations of doting self-love have all helped to crush the mass of mankind and to make liberty a convenient pretext for sham patriotism. For while rank and titles are held to be of the utmost importance, and Genius “must hide its diminished head” before them, it is, with few exceptions, very unfortunate for a nation when a man of ability, without rank or property, pushes himself forward into public notice. Alas! What unheard-of misery have thousands suffered to buy a cardinal’s hat for some scheming, obscure adventurer who longed to be ranked with princes, or to lord it over them by seizing the triple crown!

Such, indeed, has been the wretchedness that has flowed from hereditary honours, wealth and monarchy that men of lively sensibility have almost uttered blasphemy in trying to justify the ways of providence. Man has been portrayed as independent of the power of his Maker, or as a lawless planet darting out of its orbit to steal the heavenly fire of reason; and the vengeance of heaven, lurking in that subtle flame, amply punished his rashness by bringing evil into the world.

Struck by this view of the misery and disorder that pervaded society, and weary of jostling against artificial fools, Rousseau fell in love with solitude; and, being at the same time an optimist, he labours with uncommon eloquence to prove that man was by nature a solitary animal. Misled by his respect for the goodness of God — who certainly (for what man of sense and feeling can doubt it!) gave life only in order to communicate happiness — he regards evil as something positive, and as the work of man, not realizing that he was exalting one attribute at the expense of another that is equally necessary to divine perfection.

Resting on a false hypothesis, his arguments for a state of nature are plausible but unsound. I call them unsound because to claim that a state of nature is better than civilization in all its possible perfection amounts to putting supreme wisdom on trial; and the paradoxical cry that God made everything right, and that evil was brought in by the creature he formed, knowing what he was forming, is as unphilosophical as it is impious.

That wise Being who made us and set us here, when he beheld the fair idea, willed — by permitting it to be so — that our reason should be unfolded by the passions, since he could foresee that present evil would yield future good. Could the helpless creature he summoned out of nothing break loose from his providence and, without his permission, boldly learn to know good by practising evil? No. How could that energetic advocate of immortality reason so inconsistently? If mankind had stayed forever in the brutish state of nature — which not even his magic pen can depict as a condition in which a single virtue took root — it would have been plain, though not to the sensitive, unreflecting wanderer, that man was born to go round the cycle of life and death and to ornament God’s garden for some purpose hard to reconcile with his attributes.

But if, to crown the whole, rational creatures were to be produced, allowed to rise in excellence by exercising powers implanted for that purpose; if benevolence itself saw fit to call into existence a creature above the animals, one who could think and improve himself, why should that priceless gift — for a gift it was, if man was so created as to be capable of rising above the state in which sensation produced brutish ease — be called, in so many words, a curse? It might be reckoned a curse if our whole existence were limited to our time in this world; for why should the gracious fountain of life give us passions and the power of reflection only to embitter our days and fill us with mistaken notions of dignity? Why should he lead us from love of ourselves to the sublime emotions excited by the discovery of his wisdom and goodness, if these feelings were not set in motion to improve our nature, of which they form a part, and to make us capable of enjoying a more godlike share of happiness? Firmly convinced that no evil exists in the world that God did not design to take place, I build my belief on the perfection of God.
Rousseau exerts himself to prove that all WAS right originally; a crowd of authors, that all IS right now; and I, that all WILL BE right.
